fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says Gideon “…attacked their army, taking them by surprise.” (Judges 8:11). He went up by way of the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah to do it. I bet that army had no idea what hit it.
The text says, “When he had said this, their anger against him subsided.” (Judges 8:3). Gideon's answer took the fire out of the room. A few good words did what shouting never could.

The text goes the other way. After Gideon speaks, their anger against him subsided (Judges 8:3). The men of Ephraim came at him with a fight, and the storm settled down. Growing anger isn't in this passage.

The text doesn't say the anger came back. It says that after Gideon spoke, their anger against him subsided (Judges 8:3). Anger coming back isn't in this passage, baker. Ephraim cooled off like a tray finally out of the oven, and the story moves on.
Gideon doesn't ask for swords. He asks for bread (Judges 8:5). His men were exhausted, and a sword does nothing for tired. Bread is what he asked for.

The leaders of Succoth don't hand over anything. They ask, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” (Judges 8:6). Tired men asked for bread and got a question back. So the text shows no bread, and True doesn't fit.

The leaders of Succoth answer with a question: “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” (Judges 8:6). That question is what they give Gideon. They don't agree to give bread. So the statement is False.

The text says, “…the men of Penuel gave the same response as the men of Succoth.” (Judges 8:8). Gideon asked Penuel for the same thing he asked Succoth. He got the same response. Two towns, one response.

The text doesn't mention Penuel sending anyone. It says they gave the same response as the men of Succoth (Judges 8:8). Gideon had asked them for the same thing he asked Succoth, bread for his troops. That's the response they matched.
Gideon tells the men of Penuel, “When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!” (Judges 8:9). The tower is the thing he names. And he says he'll do it when he returns in triumph.

The text says, “A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen.” (Judges 8:10). Zebah and Zalmunna were at Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the armies of the people of the east. A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen fallen, baker. Let that number sit a minute.

The text says, “When Zebah and Zalmunna fled, Gideon pursued and captured these two kings of Midian…” (Judges 8:12). The kings fled, and Gideon pursued and captured them. Their entire army got routed too.
They flee, but the text says Gideon pursued and captured the two kings of Midian (Judges 8:12). Getting away isn't what happens. Their running ended with Gideon catching them.
Ephraim isn't in this verse at all, baker, not even a cameo. It says Gideon pursued and captured the two kings of Midian (Judges 8:12). The kings end up in Gideon's hands, not Ephraim's.

Not homes, friend. The young man writes down the names of the seventy-seven leaders and elders of Succoth (Judges 8:14). Homes would have needed a map, and Gideon got a list of names instead. It's a list of people, not places.

Gideon says, “They were my brothers…the sons of my mother!” (Judges 8:19). That's who the men killed at Tabor were. I think this one hurts. He adds that if they had let them live, he would not kill them.

Gideon doesn't say servants. He says, “They were my brothers…the sons of my mother!” (Judges 8:19). The kings had said the men were “each one resembling the son of a king” (Judges 8:18), and Gideon answers that they were his brothers. Brothers, not servants.
